title: Two comings of Christ and the God who is anointed
source_text: Ἔλαθε δὲ τὸν Κέλσον καὶ τὸν παρ᾿ αὐτῷ Ἰουδαῖον καὶ πάντας, ὅσοι τῷ Ἰησοῦ μὴ πεπιστεύκασιν, ὅτι αἱ προφητεῖαι δύο λέγουσιν εἶναι τὰς Χριστοῦ ἐπιδημίας, τὴν μὲν προτέραν ἀνθρωποπαθεστέραν καὶ ταπεινοτέραν, ἵνα σὺν ἀνθρώποις ὢν ὁ Χριστὸς διδάξῃ τὴν φέρουσαν πρὸς θεὸν ὁδὸν καὶ μηδενὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ βίῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀπολογίας καταλίπῃ τόπον ὡς οὐκ ἐγνωκότι περὶ τῆς ἐσομένης κρίσεως, τὴν δ᾿ ἑτέραν ἔνδοξον καὶ μόνον θειοτέραν, οὐδὲν ἐπιπεπλεγμένον τῇ θειότητι ἔχουσαν ἀνθρωποπαθές. παραθέσθαι δὲ καὶ τὰς προφητείας πολὺ ἂν εἴη· ἀρκεῖ δ᾿ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος τὸ ἀπὸ (τοῦ) τεσσαρακοστοῦ καὶ τετάρτου ψαλμοῦ, ὃς καὶ ἐπιγέγραπται πρὸς ἄλλοις εἶναι καὶ „ᾠδὴ ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ,“ ἔνθα καὶ θεὸς ἀνηγόρευται σαφῶς διὰ τούτων· „ἐξεχύθη ἡ χάρις ἐν χείλεσί σου· διὰ τοῦτο εὐλόγησέ σε ὁ θεὸς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. περίζωσαι τὴν ῥομφαίαν σου ἐπὶ τὸν μηρόν σου, δυνατὲ τῇ ὡραιότητί σου καὶ τῷ κάλλει σου, καὶ ἔντεινον καὶ κατευοδοῦ καὶ βασίλευε ἕνεκεν ἀληθείας καὶ πρᾳότητος καὶ δικαιοσύνης, καὶ ὁδηγήσει σε θαυμαστῶς ἡ δεξιά σου. τὰ βέλη σου ἠκονημένα, δυνατὲ, λαοὶ ὑποκάτω σου πεσοῦνται ἐν καρδίᾳ τῶν ἐχθρῶν τοῦ βασιλέως.“ πρόσχες δ᾿ ἐπιμελῶς τοῖς ἑξῆς, ἔνθα θεὸς εἴρηται· „ὁ θρόνος σου,“ γάρ φησιν, „ὁ θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος, ῥάβδος εὐθύτητος ἡ ῥάβδος τῆς βασιλείας σου. ἠγάπησας δικαιοσύνην καὶ ἐμίσησας ἀνομίαν· διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέ σε ὁ θεὸς ὁ θεός σου ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως παρὰ τοὺς μετόχους σου.“ καὶ κατανόει ὅτι θεῷ ὁμιλῶν ὁ προφήτης, οὗ „ὁ θρόνος“ ἐστὶν „εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος,“ καὶ „ῥάβδος εὐθύτητος ἡ ῥάβδος τῆς βασιλείας“ αὐτοῦ, τοῦτον τὸν θεόν φησι κεχρῖσθαι ὑπὸ θεοῦ, ὃς ἦν αὐτοῦ θεός· κεχρῖσθαι δὲ, ἐπεὶ „παρὰ τοὺς μετόχους“ αὐτοῦ οὗτος ἠγάπησε „δικαιοσύνην“ καὶ ἐμίσησεν „ἀνομίαν.“ καὶ μέμνημαί γε πάνυ θλίψας τὸν Ἰουδαῖον νομιζόμενον σοφὸν ἐκ τῆς λέξεως ταύτης· ὃς πρὸς αὐτὴν ἀπο ρῶν εἶπε τὰ τῷ ἑαυτοῦ ἰουδαϊσμῷ ἀκόλουθα, εἶπε πρὸς μὲν τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν εἰρῆσθαι τὸ „ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος, ῥάβδος εὐθύτητος ἡ ῥάβδος τῆς βασιλείας σου.“ πρὸς δὲ τὸν Χριστὸν τὸ „ἠγάπησας δικαιοσύνην καὶ ἐμίσησας ἀνομίαν· διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέ σε ὁ θεὸς ὁ θεός σου“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς.
pass_a_gloss: It escaped the notice (λανθάνω) of Celsus and the Jew in him and all who have not believed (πιστεύω) in Jesus that the prophecies say the comings/sojournings (ἐπιδημία) of Christ are two: the former more subject to human passion (ἀνθρωποπαθής) and humbler (ταπεινός), so that Christ being with men might teach (διδάσκω) the way (ὁδός) bearing toward God and leave to none of those in the life of men a place of defence/excuse (ἀπολογία) as not having known about the judgment (κρίσις) to be; the other glorious (ἔνδοξος) and only more divine (θεῖος), having nothing human-passioned interwoven (ἐπιπλέκω) with the divinity (θειότης). To set out (παρατίθημι) the prophecies would be much; it suffices for the present the (passage) from the forty-fourth psalm (ψαλμός), which is also inscribed (ἐπιγράφω) besides other things 'ode (ᾠδή) for the beloved (ἀγαπητός)', where also God (θεός) has been proclaimed (ἀναγορεύω) clearly through these: grace (χάρις) was poured out (ἐκχέω) on your lips; therefore God blessed (εὐλογέω) you for ever; gird (περιζώννυμι) your sword (ῥομφαία) on your thigh, mighty one (δυνατός), in your beauty (ὡραιότης) and comeliness (κάλλος), and stretch/bend (ἐντείνω) and prosper (κατευοδόω) and reign (βασιλεύω) for the sake of truth and meekness (πρᾳότης) and righteousness (δικαιοσύνη), and your right hand will guide (ὁδηγέω) you wonderfully; your arrows (βέλος) sharpened (ἀκονάω), mighty one, peoples will fall under you, in the heart of the enemies of the king. Attend (πρόσεχε) carefully to what follows, where God is said: your throne (θρόνος), O God, for ever of ever; rod (ῥάβδος) of uprightness (εὐθύτης) the rod of your kingdom (βασιλεία); you loved righteousness and hated lawlessness (ἀνομία); therefore God, your God, anointed (χρίω) you with oil (ἔλαιον) of gladness (ἀγαλλίασις) beyond your partners (μέτοχος). And observe (κατανοέω) that the prophet conversing with (ὁμιλέω) God, whose throne is for ever of ever and rod of uprightness the rod of his kingdom, says this God has been anointed by God who was his God; anointed because beyond his partners this one loved righteousness and hated lawlessness. And I remember having pressed (θλίβω) much the Jew thought wise from this passage; who, being at a loss (ἀπορέω) toward it, said what was consistent with his own Judaism (ἰουδαϊσμός): said that 'your throne, O God ... your kingdom' was spoken to the God of the universe (ὁ τῶν ὅλων θεός), and to the Christ 'you loved righteousness ... your God' and what follows.
pass_b_english: Celsus and his Jew, and all who have not believed in Jesus, have failed to notice that the prophecies speak of two comings of Christ. The first is more subject to human sufferings and more lowly, so that Christ, being with human beings, might teach the way that leads to God, and might leave no one in this human life any room to plead that he had not known of the judgment to come. The other is glorious and wholly divine, with nothing of human suffering woven into its divinity.

To set out the prophecies would take a long time. For the present it is enough to take the passage from the forty-fourth Psalm (Psalm 45 in English Bibles), which, among other things, bears the title “A song for the beloved” (Psalm 45, title). There he is also plainly proclaimed God, in these words: “Grace has been poured out on your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever. Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, in your loveliness and your beauty; and bend your bow, and prosper, and reign, for the sake of truth and meekness and righteousness, and your right hand will guide you wonderfully. Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one; peoples will fall beneath you; in the heart of the king’s enemies” (Psalm 45:2–5).

Pay careful attention to what comes next, where he is called God. “Your throne,” it says, “O God, is for ever and ever; a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:6–7). Notice that the prophet, addressing God, whose “throne” is “for ever and ever,” and the rod of whose kingdom is “a rod of uprightness,” says that this God has been anointed by God, who was his God; and that he was anointed because he, above his “companions,” loved “righteousness” and hated “lawlessness” (Psalm 45:7).

And I remember pressing the Jew who was thought wise very hard with this passage. At a loss before it, he said what fitted his own Judaism: he said that “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Psalm 45:6) was spoken to the God of the universe, and that “You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Psalm 45:7), and what follows, was spoken to the Christ.

choices.choice: LXX renumbering: Origen's 'forty-fourth psalm' is Psalm 44 LXX = Psalm 45 in English Bibles. The title 'A song for the beloved' (ᾠδὴ ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ) is LXX 44:1, the English superscription of Psalm 45 (cited inline as 'Psalm 45, title'; English Bibles give the superscription no verse number). The quoted verses are LXX 44:3-6 = English 45:2-5 and LXX 44:7-8 = English 45:6-7; Origen begins 45:2 at 'Grace has been poured out', leaving out its first clause. The wording is the Septuagint: δυνατὲ τῇ ὡραιότητί σου joins 'O mighty one' to 'in your loveliness'; ἔντεινον has no expressed object ('bend', 'stretch'); 'your bow' is supplied as the usual sense of the verb in this context. The awkward LXX order of 45:5 ('peoples will fall beneath you' between 'sharpened' and 'in the heart') is kept. 'The forty-fourth Psalm (Psalm 45 in English Bibles)' is an editorial gloss in the parenthesis only. Koetschau supplies (τοῦ) before τεσσαρακοστοῦ; followed. The staged text splits ἀπο ρῶν; read ἀπορῶν. Psalm 45:6-7 is also quoted in Hebrews 1:8-9, which Origen does not cite here; not added. 'The Christ' in the Jew's answer means the expected Messiah. μόνον θειοτέραν rendered 'wholly divine' (literally 'only more divine'). In Origen's comment παρὰ τοὺς μετόχους attaches to 'loved righteousness' ('he, above his companions, loved'), so the same word 'above' is used in the quotation and in the comment. The disputation is again Origen's own with a Jewish teacher.

'leave no one in human life any room for excuse, as though he had not known' to 'leave no one in this human life any room to plead that he had not known' (ἀπολογίας τόπον ... ὡς οὐκ ἐγνωκότι; clearer English)
'it is enough to quote the forty-fourth Psalm' to 'to take the passage from the forty-fourth Psalm' (τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ ... ψαλμοῦ: a passage, not the whole psalm)
'comeliness' to 'loveliness' and 'go on prosperously' to 'prosper' (archaisms; κατευοδοῦ)
'beyond your companions' to 'above your companions', and Origen's comment recast to 'because he, above his companions, loved righteousness' so the phrase plainly modifies 'loved' as Origen reads it
Range citations changed to en dashes to match the other Book 1 chunks; note on the omitted first clause of 45:2 added
Checked LXX Psalm 44:1, 44:3-6 and 44:7-8 against English Psalm 45 title, 45:2-5 and 45:6-7
